extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, USPTO Office of Enrollment & Discipline (OED) staff, administrative law judges, and attorneys facing USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedural rules, and factors used by the USPTO/OED and an Administrative Law Judge to determine service, default, findings of misconduct, and appropriate sanctions for registered patent practitioners under 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. parts 10 and 11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of complaint (37 C.F.R. § 11.35) / service by publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Service by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the respondent's last known address; if delivery cannot be achieved through procedures in paragraph (a) (including personal service and mail with delivery confirmation), service by publication in the Official Gazette may be initiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO should attempt certified mail with delivery confirmation (Track and Confirm) and, if that does not deliver the complaint, commence and execute service by publication (Official Gazette notices for two consecutive weeks) per § 11.35. The Tribunal found the Complainant fully complied with the requirements for proper service under § 11.35.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default for failure to answer (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If respondent does not timely answer after proper service, the allegations are deemed admitted and the Director may file a Motion for Default Judgment; the Tribunal may enter a decision by default (analogous to Fed. R. Civ. P. 55). Exhibits and the motion's assertions are incorporated into the decision by reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial decision / entry of judgment by hearing officer (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial decision of a hearing officer (Administrative Law Judge) may be entered in disciplinary proceedings under the Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AU issues an Initial Decision pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.54; appeals from the Initial Decision must be filed in duplicate with the Office of the Solicitor within 30 days as specified in § 11.55.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary sanctions available (37 C.F.R. § 11.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney who violates a Disciplinary Rule may be reprimanded, suspended, or excluded from practice before the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection among reprimand, suspension, or exclusion depends on consideration of the penalty factors in § 11.54(b) (duty violated, intent, injury, aggravating/mitigating factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty factors for determining appropriate sanction (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(1)-(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal shall consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four specific factors must be fully considered when imposing discipline. The decision applies the factors to conduct such as abandonment, failure to notify clients, issuance of bad checks, failure to return files, and failure to account for client funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to clients / core practitioner obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners owe duties to represent interests of clients competently, to keep clients informed, to return client property and files upon request, and to render appropriate accounts regarding client funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to meet these duties (e.g., allowing applications to become abandoned, not informing clients, failing to return files, failing to provide accounting) is a basis for discipline and is considered under the § 11.54 penalty factors as harming clients' IP rights and causing economic loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.23(b)(4) — dishonesty, fraud, deceit, misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuing checks that are dishonored and failing to make good on them is characterized as conduct involving dishonesty/fraud and supports a violation of this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.23(b)(5) — conduct prejudicial to administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to pay PTO fees causing examination without payment and actions that interfere with PTO processes may be prejudicial to the administration of justice and are grounds for discipline under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.23(b)(6) — conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct that adversely reflects on fitness to practice before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated misconduct such as issuing bad checks and neglecting client matters may adversely reflect on a practitioner's fitness and support exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.77(c) — neglect of legal matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to respond to PTO notices and allowing patent applications to become abandoned constitutes neglect under Rule 10.77(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.84(a) — failure to seek client's lawful objectives, failure to carry out contract, prejudicing/damaging client
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to seek lawful objectives of a client through reasonably available means; failing to carry out a contract of employment with a client; prejudicing or damaging a client during a professional relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not attempting revival, not informing clients, not returning fees or providing accounting are examples of conduct falling within Rule 10.84(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.89(c)(6) — intentional and habitual violations of disciplinary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally and habitually violating USPTO disciplinary rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pattern of repeated violations (e.g., multiple dishonored checks, repeated neglect of matters) may be characterized as intentional and habitual conduct under this rule and increases appropriateness of severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.112(c)(3) — failure to render appropriate accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to render appropriate accounts to the client regarding client funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not accounting for fees received and retained from clients (including failing to provide a full accounting upon request) violates this rule and weighs toward discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.112(c)(4) — failure to promptly deliver client property
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to promptly deliver property in the possession of the practitioner that the client is entitled to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refusal or failure to return files and documents to a former client upon request violates this rule and is an aggravating factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO fee payment rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 1.16‑1.28; § 1.22; § 1.23; § 1.53)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO charges a range of fees for patent applications (described in §§ 1.16–1.28); fees must be paid in advance pursuant to § 1.22; various payment methods are set forth in § 1.23; § 1.53 provides for assignment of a filing date without payment of the basic filing fee in limited circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced practitioners are expected to know fees are due in advance and that failure to pay may lead to abandonment. Issuance of dishonored checks to pay those fees is misconduct both because fees are due in advance and because nonpayment can prejudice clients' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of allowance / issue fee requirement (35 U.S.C. § 151)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application is allowed, a written notice specifying the issue fee is mailed; the fee must be paid within three months or the application is regarded as abandoned; remaining balance must be paid within three months of notice or the patent shall lapse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely payment of issue fees is mandatory to obtain an enforceable patent; failure to timely pay results in abandonment or lapse and may create a cloud on enforceability—an actionable injury to clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of criminal statutes as aggravating evidence (Oklahoma statutes re: bogus checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: State law (OKLA. STAT. tit. 21, §§ 1541.3–1541.4) defines false/bogus checks and prescribes criminal penalties; making/delivering checks not honored is prima facie evidence of intent to defraud unless paid within specified days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where dishonored checks meet statutory elements (e.g., two or more checks totaling $1,000+ in pursuance of a common scheme), the criminal character of the conduct is an aggravating factor supporting exclusion. The decision cites these statutes to show the seriousness of issuing bad checks to PTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of attorney discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of lawyer discipline is to protect the public and the administration of justice from lawyers who have not discharged, will not discharge, or are unlikely properly to discharge professional duties to clients, the public, the legal system, and the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary sanctions (including exclusion) are justified where they protect the public/PTO from further injury; precedents cited (cases of disbarment/suspension for abandonment/issuing bad checks) illustrate when exclusion is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and finality of disciplinary decisions (37 C.F.R. § 11.55(i) and § 11.59(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary decisions are to be published in USPTO official publications and posted in OED reading room; an Initial Decision becomes final and effective thirty days from its date in absence of a timely appeal under § 11.55(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents are informed of appeal avenues and timelines; failure to appeal results in the Initial Decision becoming final and published.
